subject: sociology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: A Marxist view of crime argues that:
options: Only the working class commit crime by nature
The law and its enforcement serve the interests of the ruling class
Crime is caused only by individual choice
There is no link between class and crime
questions.explain: Marxists argue the law is made and enforced in the interests of the powerful, while the crimes of the rich are often ignored.

questions.q: Official crime statistics may be unreliable because:
options: Some crimes go unreported and recording practices vary
questions.explain: Official statistics under-record crime because not all crimes are reported or recorded consistently.

questions.q: Crime statistics consistently show that the group most likely to be convicted of crime is:
questions.explain: Recorded statistics show young males are the group most likely to be convicted of crime.

questions.q: The 'dark figure' of crime refers to:
options: The amount of crime that is unreported and unrecorded
The most serious type of crime
questions.explain: The dark figure is the hidden volume of crime not reported to or recorded by the police.

questions.q: Durkheim, a functionalist, argued that a limited amount of crime can be:
options: Functional, e.g. reinforcing shared values and allowing social change
questions.explain: Durkheim argued some crime is inevitable and can be functional, reinforcing boundaries and enabling necessary change.

questions.q: Labelling theory, associated with Becker, argues that deviance is:
options: Created by society's reaction and the labels applied to certain acts and people
A fixed quality of an act
questions.explain: Becker argued no act is inherently deviant; deviance results from society labelling certain acts and people as deviant.

options: Disapproving looks, ridicule or family pressure
questions.explain: Informal social control uses unofficial pressures like disapproval, gossip or peer pressure rather than official agencies.

questions.q: What is the key difference between 'crime' and 'deviance'?
options: Crime breaks the law; deviance breaks norms but is not always illegal
Deviance is always more serious than crime
They mean exactly the same thing
questions.explain: Crime is behaviour that breaks the law, while deviance is behaviour that breaks social norms but may not be illegal.

questions.q: A 'victim survey' (such as the Crime Survey for England and Wales) is useful because it:
options: Only counts crimes the police record
Can reveal crimes not reported to the police
questions.explain: Victim surveys ask the public about their experiences, capturing crimes that never reached police records.

questions.q: Subcultural theories (e.g. Cohen) explain some crime as:
options: A response by some groups who form a subculture with alternative values
questions.explain: Cohen argued that some young people deprived of status form delinquent subcultures with alternative values.

questions.q: 'Formal social control' is carried out by agencies such as:
questions.explain: Formal social control is exercised by official agencies like the police, courts and prisons that enforce written rules.

questions.q: Merton's 'strain theory' explains crime as resulting from:
options: A gap between society's goals (e.g. wealth) and the legitimate means to achieve them
questions.explain: Merton argued crime arises when people cannot reach culturally approved goals (like wealth) by legitimate means, creating strain.
